:::{#exm-partial-derivative}
#### Partial derivatives of $x_1^2 x_2 + 3 x_2$

Let $f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 x_2 + 3 x_2$.
At $\vx = \tp{(1, 2)}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(1, 2) &= 1 \cd 2 + 6 \\
&= 8,
\end{aligned}
$$

and for $h \ne 0$

$$
\ba
\frac{f(1 + h, 2) - f(1, 2)}{h}
&= \frac{(1 + h)^2 \cd 2 + 6 - 8}{h}
&& \text{(substitute into } f \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{(1 + h)^2 \cd 2 - 2}{h}
&& \text{(} 6 - 8 = -2 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{(1 + 2h + h^2) \cd 2 - 2}{h}
&& \text{(expand } (1 + h)^2 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{2 + 4h + 2h^2 - 2}{h}
&& \text{(distributive law)}
\\
&= \frac{4h + 2h^2 + 2 - 2}{h}
&& \text{(reorder the terms)}
\\
&= \frac{4h + 2h^2}{h}
&& \text{(} 2 - 2 = 0 \text{)}
\\
&= 4 + 2h,
&& \text{(divide by } h \ne 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

which tends to $4$ as $h \to 0$, so $\deriv{x_1} f(1, 2) = 4$.
Holding $x_2$ fixed and differentiating in $x_1$ gives the same answer:
$\deriv{x_1} f(\vx) = 2 x_1 x_2$, which is $2 \cd 1 \cd 2 = 4$ at $\tp{(1, 2)}$.
Holding $x_1$ fixed instead gives $\deriv{x_2} f(\vx) = x_1^2 + 3$,
which is $1 + 3 = 4$ at $\tp{(1, 2)}$.

:::
